article_text:
As a teenager, Walid Raad would walk around his hometown with a camera, just trying to make some sense of the world. At a glance, the black-and-white pictures he captured then offer cool, detached views. But he quickly discovered there was only so much sense to be made of war-torn Beirut. One day, walking by a bakery, he snapped a cake displayed in the window. It was decorated with birthday wishes for someone named Hassan. Only later, developing the film at home—his dad had converted the bathroom to a darkroom, encouraging his hobby—did Raad register the date: The cake was for Hassan Nasrallah, then a rising militiaman in the Lebanese Civil War. Raad briefly fantasized about poisoning it. “But I was 15,” he told me, laughing. “I was a coward.”

Decades later, with a PhD and a MoMA retrospective under his belt, Raad returned to that image in a series of digitally fabricated birthday cakes addressed to political leaders who feel difficult to celebrate: happy birthday to Ali, Kamal, Tony, Walid; joyeux anniversaire to Yasser, Elias, Nabih, Amine. By then, Nasrallah had become the leader of Hezbollah; in 2024, he was killed in an Israeli airstrike. Raad’s colorful cakes are at once cheerful and cold—his trademark tragicomic blend of fiction and fact. In his cakes, as in so much of his work, grand political events unfold on an intimate, human scale.

Begun, in a sense, when Raad was just 15, the cake project has everything of his signature: He starts with something true—a document—then extrapolates its logic to create something fictional, maybe even a little fantastical. That method has carried him through a nearly 40-year career and counting.

His work is a standout in the main show in this year’s Venice Biennale: His paintings, drawings, and photographs of banal-seeming beds spring to life when you read a wall text claiming that they were slept in by Yasser Arafat, who “is said to have never slept in the same bed two nights in a row.” The PLO leader survived more than 40 assassination attempts, and “he could not afford to throw caution to the wind… so he lived—and slept—on the move.” Raad adds that he has spent 30 years searching for the beds Arafat slept in, drafting paintings of his mattresses and duvets that he just couldn’t seem to complete.

With the beds and cakes alike, the story unfolds quite literally along the images’ edges: The paintings of the beds are incomplete, bordered with tape and brushstrokes. The birthday cakes appear pulled out of manila envelopes along with piles of pictures, as if being entered into evidence at a trial. Raad says he is “creating the documents I wished already existed.”

SINGLING OUT RAAD’S Arafat pictures in the Biennale, the scholar Saidiya Hartman described his “belief in the imaginative and the speculative” as “critical.” Hartman has devoted her life’s work to imagining the lives of oppressed people who left limited traces in the archive—people who were silenced or illiterate, people whose voices were only recorded under conditions of coercion, or people who necessarily lived clandestine lives—like Arafat. She calls her approach “critical fabulation.”

Indeed, Raad is best known for his own method of fabulation, marrying stories and pictures, imaginations and histories. This way of working has everything to do with his primary subject: the Arab world and its politics and conflicts—particularly the Lebanese Civil War (1975—90) that unfolded in Raad’s youth. While floods of images and their competing narratives have all but defined the digital age, this battleground of misinformation has had notable consequences in the region. “During the war,” remembers Khalil Joreige, another Lebanese artist exhibiting in the Venice Biennale this year, “every militia had its own media station, television, newspaper, or radio. There was a real war of images”—a war Joreige says influenced his generation’s “sophisticated relationship to images.”

Accordingly, the Harvard art historian Carrie Lambert-Beatty has described Raad’s work as an exemplar of “parafiction,” adding that one of the most powerful things art can do is get viewers to experience a given scenario as having been true —and remind them that other worlds are possible. In her recent book on artistic research, art historian Claire Bishop singled out Raad too, noting that, while so much work in the genre reproduces the experience of information overload—think: documents in vitrines—Raad offers synthesis in the form of narrative, all without collapsing into the trope of authoritative master narratives against which so much research-based art reacts.

In my own book, Fables & Forensics, I describe Raad’s work as a kind of surrealism for the information age, noting how he gives playful form to the ordinary if dizzying glut of misinformation—but adding that he does so without ever falling into the trap of reproducing fake news. Any fact—a bed, or a birthday cake—that could be mistaken for true is of little consequence, and there are always clues as to the constructed nature of his documents; just remember to look at the edges.

Raad is best known for the work he made as a fictional collective called the Atlas Group, work that presses on photography’s fraught relationship with truth. The Group’s video Hostage: The Bachar tapes (#17 and #31) , which they attribute to the year 2000, sees Souheil Bachar narrate his experience of being held hostage in Lebanon from 1983 to ’93 alongside five Western men; he was the only Arab. Some scenes simply show Bachar against a white wall, though the video reveals itself as obviously manipulated by way of green-screened footage of Ronald Reagan. There are less obvious clues, too: If you don’t speak Arabic, you might miss how Bachar’s words are at times contradicted by the English translation.

The Group, Raad says, ran from 1989 to 2004. But dates, like all facts, are his medium. You’ll also find magazines and museums that trace the Group’s origin to 1967, the year of Raad’s birth, or to 1948, or 1945. And the Group has attributed archival images to nonexistent institutions—like the Museum of Fine Art New York. Both the Tate and the Museum of Modern Art in New York have acquired editions of his series “My Neck Is Thinner than a Hair: Engines,” but each lists the work with different dates (2000—03 and 1996—2004, respectively). And though Raad says he discontinued the Atlas Group in 2004, a work from the Group appears in the 2026 Venice Biennale catalog, with the date “printed 2023”—leaving it ambiguous as to when it was made, and whether the Group has really disbanded at all.

Still, one date is clear: Over the past two decades—since a 2005 catalyst—Raad’s work has only grown stranger. The Atlas Group primed viewers to read his documents as unstable, but the later work asks them to contend with shrunken objects, resurrected paintings, and vampires lurking in the archive. Something has shifted, and the old language of fact and fiction only scratches the surface.

IN A RESTORED 19th-century barn perched on a peak in the so-called “Irish Alps” in upstate New York, Raad keeps a meticulous archive. About an hour’s drive from Bard College, where he teaches, he and his wife duplicated the barn’s floor plan to build a second structure nearby: their home. The view from their porch is straight out of a Hudson River School painting, and meeting him for the first time feels like a peek behind the curtain: For over 20 years, he has diligently hidden his likeness from all corners of the internet, populating the algorithm with other faces to throw it off his scent. He explained his evasiveness in one word—“phobia”—but it was hard not to see it as just one more way Raad uses photography to make the world feel larger and stranger, rather than to try to “capture” it. In person, he is warm and welcoming, serving homemade tabbouleh and hummus “the right way”—with sumac and olive oil.

In the barn, Raad has assiduously organized ephemeral materials like wall labels from his exhibitions and name cards from dinners he’s attended, all fodder that may or may not become an artwork in the future. A strappy leather portfolio contained his juvenilia, including those pictures he made as a teenager. He went to high school in Boston—“They had a darkroom and they had a basketball team, so it was great,” he said—where he made pictures in the style of Cindy Sherman, Diane Arbus, Garry Winogrand, Stephen Shore, Henri Cartier-Bresson, and Lucas Samaras. Raad was able to approximate all of their styles, but what he carried from the exercise most clearly was the experience of embodying a persona from behind the camera.

In 1985, Raad started his undergraduate degree at the Rochester Institute of Technology, where he majored in medicine before switching to photography. While there, he won his first photography prize, for a work he made under the pseudonym P.X. Chesterfield, inspired by a real US Marine Corps general, P.X. Kelley, whose name he thought sounded cool. Soon after, he enrolled in the University of Rochester’s “Cultural and Visual Studies” PhD program, which sported rising-star faculty: Craig Owens, Kaja Silverman, Douglas Crimp. It “was psychoanalysis, linguistics, and Marxism,” Raad explained. “The holy trinity.” For Raad, persona, theory, and photography were starting to converge.

As a student, Raad visited and photographed Beirut each summer, a practice he continues to this day. Back home, he tried aping observational techniques from Diane Arbus or Eugène Atget that he’d observed in photography magazines his dad gave him. But he found that “even something as simple as using a tripod was impossible… in a city that’s full of snipers.” He wasn’t making war photography, either, never capturing the actions, always the aftermath.

After taking pictures of detonated bombs, however, Raad was often left with the sense that something was missing, so he started getting his hands on the pictures—circling detritus with a red pencil. Kernels of his most famous works are palpable in his teenage years, which seems appropriate for an artist who describes himself as starting out with an interest in “a certain way of thinking about violence and trauma.” Versions of those red circles recur in the Atlas Group’s Let’s Be Honest, the Weather Helped (1998/2006), black-and-white snapshots of Beirut marked with brightly colored dots corresponding to the code system that ammunition manufacturers use to identify cartridges and shells—and thus, indirectly, their makers. In Raad’s hands, the dots read as much confetti as forensic notations.

Under the Atlas Group, Raad was crafting personas like the gambling historian Dr. Fadl Fakhouri and the unlucky police detective Yussef Bitar—“very serious, very professional people,” he explained—the kind likely to leave behind official documents. But eventually, he found the Atlas Group “somewhat limited,” and became interested in showing how “violence has more insidious effects than we know.” Besides, he added, by the early aughts, he felt that “the language of maps and archives had been exhausted.”

RAAD’S THINKING BEGAN to shift after meeting, in the early ’90s, the Lebanese writer and artist Jalal Toufic while working on a video project about the occupation of South Lebanon. He started reading Toufic’s books, which he found difficult to parse at first, but eventually, he found Forthcoming (2000). That book includes the story of a classically trained photographer who can’t stop making blurry pictures of buildings in Beirut. Raad instantly recognized himself.

“I freaked out,” Raad told me. “It was as if he could hear my internal monologue.” He thought about how certain photographic tropes—something as simple as a tripod—had been rendered unavailable to him in wartime Beirut, but soon was thinking more expansively about all that violence had withdrawn from him. His trinity-training in Rochester had taught him that “language, psyche, the economy… that’s the stuff of the world.” Toufic, he said, gave him language for “a different place that I’d never been introduced to.”

Toufic has influenced almost everything Raad has made since that encounter. “I’m embarrassed by how much I talk about that guy,” he told me. “It’s as if I cannot have a thought without passing through him.” Of lasting impact was Toufic’s concept of “withdrawal,” spelled out most explicitly in The Withdrawal of Tradition Past a Surpassing Disaster (2009) but also addressed in earlier essays. In it, he describes the sorts of immaterial losses that can arise in the wake of major cultural upheavals—the ways that rituals and forms can become unavailable or lose their potency when the society that gave rise to them is changed irreversibly by disaster.

Tradition, Toufic theorizes, might be clung to steadfastly in the aftermath of disaster, as in the revival of Orthodox Judaism in the wake of the Holocaust; or it might be suppressed entirely, as in versions of modernism that, also in the wake of the world wars, try in vain to imagine a clean slate and abolish antecedents. When a tradition comes back to life in a new context, something is always off: Toufic calls the act a “resurrection,” because the tradition is not alive so much as undead. The artist’s job is to make this withdrawal palpable—to make the absence present, “like the mirror in vampire films”; for Toufic, only those who try and fail to resurrect withdrawn tradition “may become truly absolutely modern.”

This concept of withdrawal informed the pivotal work Raad showed at the Arab world’s first white cube gallery, Sfeir-Semler Gallery, which opened in 2005. He’d declined the invitation several times before eventually acquiescing in 2008, sensing that something seemed off. When he arrived at the gallery, he found that the Atlas Group’s work he shipped had been shrunk to 1/100th of its original size. When I pressed Raad on how this could be possible, he said that “there are conditions under which your own work is no longer available to you, and your only relation to it feels distorted.” For him, this is not “a symptom, and not a metaphor.” It’s also “not quantum,” nor a condition of “one’s psyche, material conditions, or language”—it is, he said, “withdrawal.” Withdrawal is also the very reason he could not complete those Arafat bed paintings.

The affinities between Raad and Toufic are striking enough that more than one person has confessed their suspicion that Toufic is simply another of Raad’s personas—a theory that would require an elaborate ruse if true, with Raad hiring a body double to appear alongside him at public events. But while Raad is undoubtedly skilled at crafting fictions and personas, he is less interested in pranks than in fables—in what happens when something is imagined as having been true rather than in trickery and illusion.

AFTER THE ATLAS GROUP mined the archive and rendered it strange, Raad’s work went beyond scrambling fact and fiction and toward something more like magical realism. Along the way, photography—which is so hard to read without thinking about truth—became less central. Better be watching the clouds again and again (2000/2017) is a series of collages attributed to a fictional Lebanese Army officer named Fadwa Hassoun, who’d trained as a botanist. During the war, Hassoun assigned politicians flowers as code names, and the work that tells her story features black-and-white portraits of Benjamin Netanyahu, Saddam Hussein, Ronald Reagan, and more with their heads crowned by colorful petals, their legs made to look like stems.

More recently, Raad collaborated with graphic designer Pierre Huyghebaert on I thought I’d escape my fate (again) (2025), an installation that gathers statements from people involved in exhibitions and programs canceled over expressions of solidarity with Palestine. Printed, cut out, and taped low along a gallery baseboard, these quotes are hard to read without crouching. What catches the eye instead are the colored strips of tape running across the wall, like placeholders for the artworks that never got to hang in such a space. It’s another example of how disaster can show up in art sideways, of Toufic’s idea that conflict leaves traces that are visible in artworks and cultural traditions only in the form of absence—that a “truly modern” artwork might make this absence visible.

Toufic’s vampire-mirror idea resurfaces too in other works of Raad’s on display in Venice, alongside the Arafat pieces. Copies of stolen Arab and Turkish artworks appear painted on the undersides of wooden pallets. Here, as in several recent works, the vampire Raad holds a mirror up to is modern Arab art itself, which lately has undergone a period of “rediscovery,” to use the art world’s favorite term—or, resurrection. When the Lebanese Civil War ended in 1990, a wall text informs, militias sold off weapons, many of which found their way to the Balkans; the Yugoslav Wars, then, were fought partly with Lebanese arms. The text adds that the painted pallets were recently found in Ljubljana, at the Moderna Galerija—where, conveniently, he just closed a mid-career retrospective.

Next spring, at Paula Cooper Gallery in New York, Raad will place a vintage VW Beetle on its back in the gallery like a dying bug—a reference to “flying Volkswagens,” as American soldiers called the artillery shells they fired on Beirut in the 1980s. Surrounding them on the walls will be reproductions of handwritten notes left on bombs by soldiers in various languages, including English, Russian, Arabic, Hebrew, and French—like xoxo, or the dildo of consequences rarely arrives lubed, or from silicon valley with love. Raad found images on Reddit posted by braggadocious soldiers from around the world, and then exaggerated the size and changed the color of their inscriptions. There isn’t a whole lot of fiction or fantasy in this one: Sometimes, the facts are strange enough.

article_text:
There’s a jump scare about 30 minutes into the glossy romantic drama Love of Your Life that’s about as effective as anything you’ll see in a horror movie this year.

The film is focused on the life and loves of Maya (Margaret Qualley), a twentysomething Boston nurse who meet-cutes with the nerdy and idiosyncratic Charlie (Gabriel Basso) during the purchase of a nightstand. We follow the initial giddy rush of their courting as they progress all the way to an impromptu wedding over the course of a few years, marked by Maya’s change in age announced in text. But just as we’re about to process the unsettling introduction of Charlie using Chekhov’s inhaler, a news report interrupts the sunny tone. Spoiler: it’s March 2020.

Rather like the ending of the otherwise anodyne romance Remember Me which shows Robert Pattinson’s character looking out of the World Trade Center on 9/11 (!), it’s revealed that we are in fact watching a Covid movie, at least for the first act, which ends, unsurprisingly, with the death of Charlie. This then propels Maya on to an international odyssey from Portugal to England to Japan as she tries to figure out who she is without the man she thought she would grow old with (it involves what’s described as “solitary hedonism” AKA one-night stands with guys who have tattoos and croissants in the bath). That journey pushes her away from her best friend, played by Patrick Schwarzenegger, and mother-in-law, played by Catherine Keener, and toward Aaron Pierre’s charming single father.

It’s Eat, Grieve, Love which is by no means a bad thing given how few mainstream films attempt to zero in on the vast lives of women both in and out of relationships (I remain a staunch defender of Ryan Murphy’s prettified yet emotionally resonant adaptation of a book I am otherwise unbothered by). There’s also a bit of How to Be Single (minus the bawdy humour), another film I’m often defending or at least drawing attention to and there’s something admirably ambitious about settling in with a female protagonist for such a long period of time to see how they live and learn after a loss many of us couldn’t imagine surviving.

The script was the subject of a heated auction back in 2024, sparking interest from studios like Paramount and unlikely names such as Taylor Sheridan, who usually prefers his female characters blond and hypersexual. It sold for $2m, a virtually unheard of amount for a spec script in this climate, recalling the mostly long-gone glory days of someone like Shane Black or Paul Verhoeven. It sold to Ryan Gosling, as producer, and Amazon and comes from the Nyad writer Julia Cox although it often feels like it was adapted from an elevated beach read.

It’s a sumptuous trip around the world and through the grieving process that’s mostly smooth sailing, steered by a director who knows how to fully transport us. Cinematographer turned film-maker Rachel Morrison went from capturing the small (Fruitvale Station) to the epic (Black Panther) and she’s brought both to her work as director. I was disappointed her excellent boxing drama The Fire Inside didn’t reach a wider audience and while I understand the unwillingness to bet on a genre more commonly suited to streaming, it’s a shame Amazon isn’t giving this one a wider big-screen rollout especially given how lush so much of it looks (it’ll have a token week in cinemas before it’s next to your shampoo order).

There’s perhaps not quite as much depth or texture as one might hope, especially as a rambling third act scrambles for something close to profundity, and the finished product, together with its weirdly muted rollout, might not quite justify the intensity, or the high price, involved with the auction. But it is refreshing to see a battle over a grounded drama rather than heightened genre for once (I’m assuming the Covid angle is what launched it into the marketplace).

It also gives Qualley one of her most grounded roles too, a challenge for the actor to play a real, relatable person after mainly doing the opposite in films like The Substance, Poor Things, Honey, Don’t and Blue Moon. It’s an easy fit for her, more so than her last attempt, Maid, and we buy her grand gamut of grief (devastation, frustration, horniness) without the need for her to histrionically overplay the life-changing horror of it, also helped by Basso’s believably specific performance, someone who is admittedly hard to forget.

If Schwarzenegger feels entirely miscast as her bestie and their lived-in long-term dynamic hard to buy then a more neatly suited Pierre more than makes up for it. He’s another actor who has mostly been limited to something else – action, an American accent – but he’s an incredibly charismatic romantic lead here and it’s not hard to buy how he might find a way to break down the walls of Maya, that have been understandably built up so very high.

Their electric chemistry helps to power the film as it plods into a final third that feels considerably more aimless than it should. The journey we take with Maya has been in many ways such an epic one, in both literal and emotional scope, and it feels like after all of that, we should be taken somewhere more meaningful and left with insights more incisive than what we end up with. For a film so set on exploring the monumental sweep of both love and life, the end result soothes rather than soars.

Love of Your Life is premiering at the Toronto film festival; it will be on limited release in cinemas on 7 October and on Prime Video on 14 October

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们对这个项目兴奋了一段时间。当我们看到第一剪时，所有人都被这部电影的震撼力量和独创性惊艳到了，”DR Sales 执行制片人金·克里斯蒂安森说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一部融合了剧情、纪录片与幕后花絮的独特作品，《父亲的房子》（Faderhuset）审视了激进丹麦基督教教派“父亲的房子”（Faderhuset）内部的操纵、虐待以及常常伴随的暴力。三名曾加入该派别的成员揭露了这个现已解散的教派内部运作内幕，据报道，驱魔、说方言和激进基督教曾是其日常生活的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这场封闭派别中，三位主角生命中的决定性时刻通过成熟演员的重现演绎重新复活，并在真正的昔日成员指导下完成。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在一场元叙事实践中，蒂虹饰演自20世纪90年代起一直领导“父亲的房子”直至该宗教社群2013年正式关闭的魅力型领袖露丝·埃文森（现名露丝·克里斯蒂安森）。丹席克饰演前成员杰里，劳拉·克伦堡·凯尔（《一个幸运的人》、《当阳光照耀》）则饰演卡米拉——她在“父亲的房子”逗留了7年，随后决裂并创立了旨在帮助人们离开此类派别社群的非政府组织 InsideOut。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为什么要请来崔娜·蒂虹和大卫·丹席克？穆尔瓦德向《综艺》透露，这部电影的起点是前成员卡米拉·路易丝·约翰逊所著的一本书，正是这本书激发了她对“邪教、群体动态以及为什么自由世界里的人渴望归属感”至愿意放弃自己生命的兴趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "被穆尔瓦德形容为整个电影制作过程中的“重要把关人”的卡米拉，随后将导演们引见给了该教派的其他前成员，他们“慷慨地分享了自己的经历”并为剧本做出了贡献。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了避免陷入“作为纪录片导演那种漫长而孤独的过程”，一旦影片的混合概念成型，穆尔瓦德便拉上了克福德。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我觉得它非常具有原创性和趣味性，这让我有机会以一种全新的方式工作，”这位曾执导翠贝卡电影节入选片、索尼经典发行的《失落的达芬奇》的导演说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "曾剪辑穆尔瓦德卡罗维发利获奖纪录片《美好生活》及克福德备受赞誉的《空投》的尼尔森也加入了进来，迎来了他的首次导演执我体验。“我基本上就是《谋杀绿脚趾》里的那张地毯——那个把整个房间串联起来的东西，”他开玩笑说，随后承认：“这确实让我对[导演工作]上了瘾。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当被问及他们为何选择将剧情片与纪录片融为一体时，联合导演们表示：“最吸引我们的是来自‘父亲的房子’那些光怪陆离的内部故事。然而，由于这些时刻没有任何影像资料，我们知道自己不想依赖传统的、以采访为主导的纪录片。与此同时，我们又想避免拍成一部把真实人类经历强行塞入刻板情节的标准剧情片。我们想要两全其美。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一名剪辑师，尼尔森从他参与卡斯帕·阿斯特鲁普的纪录片《中松博士的发明》的经历中汲取了灵感。在该片中，这位古怪的日本发明家想将自己童年的一刻虚构化，用演员导演并亲自在镜头前指导了一场戏。“这真是不可思议的搞笑而又超现实，这种带有元叙事层面的方法深深留在了亚当心中，”联合导演们说道。他们同样受到了考塞尔·本·哈里亚的混合形式影片《四女儿》的启发。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们意识到这种方法可以解锁我们自己的叙事，于是决定尝试一下，”他们在阐述自己的技术时说。“我们用演员崔娜·蒂虹和劳拉·克伦堡·凯尔与真正的昔日成员卡米拉·约翰逊进行了一次试拍。卡米拉与演员之间的化学反应堪称电光石火，但这次测试还揭示了更深层次的东西：它成了一种深刻的方式，暴露出我们在制作电影时——无论是剧情片还是纪录片——是如何操纵现实的。通过拉开我们自己创作过程的帷幕，这种混合风格使我们能够摆脱线性时间轴，转而围绕纯粹的情感和心理结构来构建电影，”这三位导演表示。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "合作剧本分阶段编写，联合导演们将他们的剧情素材调整为前教派成员详细描述的真实场景，而演员们则不得不学习一种新的[宗教]语言，“其中上帝、魔鬼、赞美、天使等等占据了主导地位。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“丰富而疯狂”的素材", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们得到的素材既丰富又疯狂，”电影制片人表示，他们决定“在场景中寻找两难困境——也就是前成员们为了获得领袖或群体的信任而不得不放弃自我的时刻、摩擦与存在主义怀疑的时刻。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当被问及他们对“天父之家”的个人看法时，穆尔瓦德、科弗德和尼尔森表示：“说实话，‘天父之家’本质上并不比历史上许多其他宗教宗派或邪教更糟糕。真正让我们感到恐惧的，不仅仅是这个群体本身，而是人类为了绝望地寻求爱、接纳和归属感，竟然会做出多么极端的事情。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他们接着说道：“看着银幕并心想‘这种事绝不会发生在我身上’，这固然令人感到宽慰。但现实是，我们大多数人都曾身处某种情境——无论是在恋爱关系、工作还是社交圈中——底线被突破，而我们远远超出了自己对是非曲直的判断。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "归根结底，这三位导演希望他们的电影“能够引发一场关于操纵行为的讨论”，“引导观众开始更多地倾听自己的直觉。它存在是有原因的，”他们说。“到头来，你可以扰乱人们的思绪，你可以对他们进行煤气灯式的精神操控，但你无法干涉他们的直觉。这就是我们希望[观众]能够带走的——相信那个内在的声音。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一部90分钟的电影或两集剧集进行推介，“天父之家”由佩妮莱·罗斯·格伦克耶（Pernille Rose Grønkjær）和马尔特·科赫（Malthe Koch）为丹麦纪录片公司（Danish Documentary）以及北欧公共广播公司DR、NRK和SVT制作。丹麦上映计划通过Camera Film于11月19日进行。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Copenhagen-based DR Sales , the international distributor of Oscar-winning doc “Mr Nobody Against Putin” and Sundance winner “A New Kind of Wilderness,” has boarded Denmark’s “Father’s House,” starring David Dencik (“No Time to Die,” “The Chestnut Man”) and Trine Dyrholm (“The Danish Woman,” “Queen of Hearts”).

Selected for the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival international documentary competition and IDFA’s Signed section, “Father’s House” sees Dencik and Dyrholm acting in the reenactment scenes of a film which homes in on manipulation in a religious sect.

Related Stories

Amy Poehler's 'Dig' Adds Max Greenfield, Jason Mantzoukas, Noma Dumezweni and More (EXCLUSIVE)

Noah Wyle Named People’s 2026 Sexiest Man Alive

“Father’s House” is co-directed by multi-awarded doc specialists Andreas Koefoed (“The Lost Leonardo,” “Music for Black Pigeons”), Eva Mulvad (“Enemies of Happiness,” “The Good Life”) and editor Adam Nielsen (“The Investigation,” “The Letter Room”).

“We have been very excited about this project for some time. Once we saw the first cut, we were all blown away by how powerful and original the film is,” said DR Sales Executive Producer Kim Christiansen.

A distinctive mix of fiction, documentary and making off, “Father’s House” (“Faderhuset”) looks at manipulation, abuse and often violence inside the radical Danish Christian sect Faderhuset, as three former members expose the inner workings of the now defunct sect where exorcism and speaking in tongues and militant Christianity were, reportedly, part of everyday life.

Defining moments in the lives of the three characters within that closed sect are brought back to life via reenactments from established actors, under the guidance of the real former members.

In a meta exercise. Dyrholm plays the charismatic leader Ruth Evensen (now Ruth Kristiansen) who led Fathers House since the 1990s until its official closure as a religious congregation in 2013. Dencik is the former member Jerry and Laura Kronborg Kjær (“A Fortunate Man,” “When the Sun Shines”) Camilla who stayed seven years within Father’s House before breaking away and setting up the NGO-InsideOut to help people leave such sectarian communities.

Why Bring in Trine Dyrholm and David Dencik? Mulvad told Variety that the starting point to the film was a book written by former member Camilla Louise Johnson which sparked her interest in “cults, group dynamics and why people in a free world long to belong,” to the extent of surrendering their own lives.

Depicted by Mulvad as “an important gatekeeper” throughout the filmmaking process, Camilla then introduced the directors to other former members of the sect who “shared their experience in a generous way” and contributed to the script.

To avoid getting into “the long and lonely process of being a documentary director,” Mulvad rallied to her idea Koefoed, once the film’s hybrid concept was in place.

“I found it very original and playful, and it gave me the opportunity to work in a new way,” said the helmer of the Tribeca-selected Sony Classics release “The Lost Leonardo.”

Nielsen who had edited Mulvad’s Karlovy Vary winning doc “The Good Life” and Koefoed’s acclaimed “The Arms Drop,” joined, enjoying his first directing gig. “I was basically the rug from “The Big Lebowski” – the one tying the room together,” he quipped, before admitting: “It definitely gave me a taste for [directing].

Quizzed about their choice to mix fiction and documentary, the co-helmers said, “What interested us most were the bizarre, insider stories from Father’s House. However, since no footage of those moments existed, we knew we didn’t want to rely on a traditional, interview-driven documentary. At the same time, we wanted to avoid a standard fiction film that forces real human experiences into a rigid plot. We wanted the best of both worlds.”

As an editor, Nielsen took inspiration from his work on Kaspar Astrup’s documentary “The Invention of Dr. Nakamats” in which the eccentric Japanese inventor wanted to fictionalise a moment from his childhood, staging a scene with actors, while directing it himself on camera.“It was incredibly funny and surreal, and that meta-layered approach stayed with Adam,” said the co-helmers who were also inspired by a similar hybrid form in Kaouther Ben Haria’s “Four Daughters.”

“We realised this approach could unlock our own narrative, so we decided to test it,” they said, outlining their technique. “We ran a pilot with actors Trine Dyrholm and Laura Kronborg Kjær interacting with the real ex- member Camilla Johnson. The dynamic between Camilla and the actors was electric, but the test also revealed something deeper: it became a profound way to expose how we manipulate reality when making films, whether fiction or documentary. By pulling back the curtain on our own process, the hybrid style allowed us to break free from a linear timeline and instead build the film around a purely emotional and psychological structure,” said the directing trio.

The collaborative script was written in different steps, with the co-helmers adapting their fiction material to the real scenes depicted in detail by the former sect members, while the actors had to learn a new [religious] language, “where God, devil, praise, angels and so on take a dominant space.”

‘Rich and Crazy’ Material

“The material we got was rich and crazy,” said the filmmakers who decided “to look for dilemmas in the scenes, moments where the ex-members had to give up themselves to gain the trust of the leader or the group, moments of friction and existential doubt.”

Asked about their personal take on Father’s House, Mulvad, Koefoed and Nielsen said, “Honestly, Father’s House isn’t fundamentally worse than many other religious sects or cults throughout history. What truly terrified us wasn’t just the group itself, but rather the lengths to which we as humans will go in our desperate search for love, acceptance and a sense of belonging.”

They went on: “It’s comforting to look at the screen and think, ‘That would never happen to me.’ But the reality is that most of us have found ourselves in situations- – whether in relationships, jobs, or social circles – where boundaries were crossed, and we went far beyond our own sense of right and wrong.”

Ultimately, the directing trio hope their film “will start a conversation about manipulative behaviour” and “lead the audience to start listening more to their gut feeling. It’s there for a reason,” they said. “At the end of the day, you can mess with people’s heads, you can gaslight them, but you can’t mess with their intuition. That’s what we want [the audience] to take away-trusting that inner voice.”

Shopped as a 90-minute film or two-part series, “Father’s House” was produced by Pernille Rose Grønkjær and Malthe Koch for Danish Documentary and Nordic public broadcasters DR, NRK and SVT. The Danish release via Camera Film is slated for Nov. 19.

"作为一名经济自由主义者，巴罗佐对此并不买账，会议气氛也随之变得白热化。“他非常愤怒，尽管他为建立一个统一的欧洲做出了种种尝试，但比如爱沙尼亚的人民仍然不愿意观看一部来自葡萄牙的电影，”蒙吉乌说，他对这种态度的沮丧再次浮现于表面。“一个欧洲？这当然是正确的方向。但距离这些人互相交战、一切都建立在单一国家和单一文化基础之上，至今也才过去了短短几十年代。从历史角度来讲，那并不是很久以前的事。让我们朝着那个新方向前进，没问题——但你不能假装我们已经到达了终点。”", article_text:
‘P ffff!” Cristian Mungiu lets out an exasperated sigh. We are sitting in the basement of a London hotel, at the end of a long morning of back-to-back interviews for the Romanian film-maker, and his press handler has just snuck into the room to remind him of his next appointment across town. But Mungiu blanks him and leans on to his table, because he wants to tell one more story.

In 2013, Mungiu was part of a delegation of European auteurs who travelled to Brussels to meet the then president of the European Commission, José Manuel Barroso. At the time, the EU and US were in talks to slash barriers to trade between the two economic blocs, and the film-makers were lobbying the Commission to spare their industry from the deal .

If countries weren’t allowed to subsidise their own productions, one argument went, European cinema would become a stolid mush of homogenised co-productions – “Europudding”, as people called it at the time. To those ends, they would no longer be able to create national dramas like Mungiu’s own 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days , a riveting abortion thriller set in cold war-era Bucharest that had won the Palme d’Or at Cannes in 2007.

Barroso, an economic liberal, was not impressed, and the meeting became heated. “He was very angered that in spite of all his attempts to create a united Europe , people in, say, Estonia were still reluctant to watch a film from Portugal,” says Mungiu, his own frustration with that attitude bubbling to the surface once more. “One Europe? It’s the right direction, sure. But it has still only been tens of years since all these people were fighting each other and everything was based on national states and national cultures. Historically speaking, that wasn’t a long time ago. Let’s go in that new direction, fine – but you can’t pretend we’ve already got there.”

I suspect Mungiu is keen to tell this story for two reasons. His latest film, Fjord, is about people from different European cultures coming together – but also about how different national identities continue to keep them apart. Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu, a Romanian-Norwegian couple with five young children, move from Bucharest to her native country in the icy north. The Gheorghius are devout evangelical Christians, yet the liberally minded locals welcome the newcomers with open arms in spite of their anti-modern way of life. Mihai, an engineer, and nurse Lisbet both find employment, the children settle at school; they make friends with their neighbours, headteacher Mats, lawyer Mia and their teen-rebel daughter, Noora.

But when a PE teacher notices bruises on the body of the Gheorghius’ eldest daughter, Elia, tolerance turns to distrust. Child protection services become involved, and Mihai does his family no favours when he denies that he has abused his children, but insists that a slap on the bottom can sometimes be necessary, to teach that “you can’t escape punishment when you’re wrong”. Soon, the state separates the parents from their children, including their newborn baby, and the Gheorghius’ family values become a diplomatic incident.

Since his 2007 Cannes triumph, Mungiu has made several films that deal with the social consequences of globalisation and migration – a particularly prescient subject for a Romanian, given that 25% of his compatriots live abroad. Beyond the Hills (2012) and Graduation (2016) revolved around characters who have returned from working abroad or are desperate to leave Romania to do so; 2022’s RMN dealt with protests over Sri Lankan migrant workers in a rural village in Transylvania.

But Fjord – and this is the other reason Mungiu’s encounter with Barroso is relevant – is not just a film about globalisation, but also one shaped by a globalised economy. It is an international co-production of the kind that Mungiu’s delegation had warned the European Commission about, shot in Norway and edited in Romania, its sound designed in Finland and mixed in Denmark. It’s also his first English-language film, and the first to star two Oscar-nominated A-listers, Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve. Mungiu almost sounds embarrassed about it: “It has a lot to do with the financing system,” he says. “I’m not a big fan of this system, to be honest,” he adds, sheepishly.

Yet Fjord is no Europudding, but something altogether classier and more refined – more of a Euro-flan, with a bitter layer permeating the sweetness. It still has all the stylistic hallmarks that have made Mungiu the standout film-maker of the Romanian new wave: a pacing that makes viewers feel they are living the Gheorghius’ ordeal in something like real time , but also a renunciation of manipulative edits or closeups that could coerce us into fully taking their point of view.

Fjord is cinema as Rorschach test. How the bruise on Elia’s back came about is never fully explained. Whether you are more outraged by the Norwegian state’s dogmatic liberalism or by the Romanians’ disciplinarian ways is designed to tell you more about yourself than the characters on screen. “We watch too many stories that are there just to confirm to you that you are on the right side of things,” Mungiu says. “In the last 10, 20 years we started making a lot of films in which everything is clear and the author takes you by the hand and tells you what you need to believe: they are the good guys, they are the bad guys.”

Fjord won the Palme d’Or at Cannes this year, putting Mungiu in the distinguished league of directors who have won the most prestigious prize in arthouse cinema twice, which includes such luminaries as Michael Haneke, Francis Ford Coppola and Ken Loach. Ironically, some of the film’s most positive reviews since were from Norway, he says, where “nobody considered the film a criticism of Norwegian society, not even [Norway’s child welfare authority] Barnevernet”.

But not everyone at Cannes thought Fjord was a deserving winner. The two films that scored highest with the critics , interestingly, were also Euro-flans: Polish director Paweł Pawlikowski’s German-language Fatherland and Russian film-maker Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur, a coproduction between France, Latvia and Germany. In Mungiu’s native Romania, some critics felt the film was unduly forgiving of corporal punishment. In France, one critic complained about Fjord’s “proto-Nazi” portrayal of the child-protection officers. “Beneath its veneer of a fair film, beneath its stated desire to depict two opposing value systems, Cristian Mungiu constantly chooses sides,” wrote David Fonseca in Le Rayon Vert . The trial the film puts on, it declared, was “a sham”.

Such withering invective seems over the top, and at the very least ignores the film’s subplot – a nascent homoerotic relationship between the Gheorghiu’s eldest daughter and her neighbour-classmate that shows up Mihai’s autocratic rule within his family. But it’s probably fair to say that Fjord is a conservative film with a small “c”: not in the brash and hectoring way that modern conservative parties are, but doubtful and self-questioning, yet conservative nonetheless in its instinctive distrust of the state.

“I come from this very authoritarian society and I’ve seen that it’s not good to give people too much power because there are natural tendencies to abuse it,” Mungiu says. “I want to make sure that we don’t get back to this situation in which somebody knows better than us what’s good for us – I’ve been there.” He chuckles sardonically. “I have so many fans in France who are communists. Well, I’m so sorry that they didn’t come to spend the 70s with us in Romania. Not to mention the 50s!”

Mungiu does not want to be labelled a conservative. “The fact that I’m presenting these arguments without commenting doesn’t mean for a second that I’m in any way a supporter of conservative values and of all the intolerance that they carry.” His criticism of liberal societies such as Norway, he insists, is above all due to the fact that he has higher expectations of them. “They are more educated, so they should be the ones initiating a dialogue with the other side. The conversation starts when you have this patience to listen.”

In one scene in the film, one of the Gheorghius’ daughters is revealed to have told a classmate that their sexuality was an entry ticket to hell. I ask Mungiu how much patience that young girl should have, listening to these bigots. “I’m aware that it’s more complicated in reality,” he concedes. “But you should ask yourself, why are we in this situation? After years and years of trying to make the world a more liberal place, we ended up by having a more illiberal kind of world. Haven’t we maybe exaggerated in some areas with the way we were trying to force things? It’s like trying to ripen a banana with a hairdryer. It doesn’t work like that. People need time.”

Later, I check the box office figures for Fjord and realise that the film beat Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey to reach No 1 in Norway on its opening day, which would surely have pleased José Manuel Barroso. In 2026, the idea that Estonians may flock to cinemas to watch a film from Portugal no longer seems quite so absurd. Meanwhile, in Hungary and Serbia, Romania’s neighbouring countries, young voters have toppled Christian nationalist strongmen. People need more time, until they don’t.

Fjord is released in the UK and Ireland on 13 November; and in Australia on 28 January 2027

article_text:
Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another has been the talk of the town since its wide release last month—from critics to filmmakers to audiences, the reception has been nothing short of euphoric. Loosely inspired by Thomas Pynchon’s novel Vineland , the film opens in an unspecified present, detailing the activities of a militant group led by a Black revolutionary (played by Teyana Taylor). Years after her disappearance, her partner (Leonardo DiCaprio) and their daughter (newcomer Chase Infiniti) are hunted down by an old enemy, Sean Penn’s Colonel Steven J. Lockjaw. The chase takes them across California, with an assortment of other characters becoming embroiled along the way.

The movie is an unabashedly fun, feel-good action flick—one that also calls back to films as disparate as The Searchers , Commando , and Running on Empty . But is it among the greatest of the decade, as some have claimed? Film Comment Editors Clinton Krute and Devika Girish invited critics and programmers Miriam Bale and Adam Piron on the Podcast to discuss the film’s successes and failures, how it fits into PTA’s larger body of work, and its engagement with American history and the present. If there’s one thing the four agreed on, it’s that One Battle After Another is indeed a “ very rich text.”

article_text:
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the latest entry in the Hunger Games film franchise, based on Suzanne Collins’s 2025 novel.

Lionsgate has released a set of character posters that offer a closer look at the personalities in this prequel series, which stars Joseph Zada as a young Haymitch Abernathy.

Directed by Francis Lawrence and written by Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie, the film is set to open in theaters on November 20.

RELATED: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Red Carpet Photos: All Of Joseph Zada & Mckenna Grace’s Looks From Press Tour

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping follows sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Zada) from District 12, beginning on the morning of the reaping for the 50th Annual Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, the biggest Games yet with twice as many tributes.

Set in the world of Panem 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games , the story follows Haymitch into the arena, where he forms an unlikely alliance with fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Grace) and joins a coalition determined to challenge the Capitol’s control under President Snow (Ralph Fiennes).

As the competition unfolds, Haymitch risks everything to take down the Games from within the arena — setting in motion the rebellion that will change Panem forever.

RELATED: Everything We Know About The ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Movie So Far

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping stars Joseph Zada (Haymitch), Mckenna Grace (Maysilee), Glenn Close (Drusilla), Ralph Finneas (President Snow), Billy Porter (Magno), Maya Hawke (Wiress), Elle Fanning (Effie), Percy Daggs IV (Ampert), Whitney Peak (Lenore Dove), Lili Taylor (Mags), Kiran Culkin (Caesar Flickerman), Kelvin Harrison Jr (Beetee), Jesse Plemons (Plutarch), Ben Wang (Wyatt), among others.

article_text:
News

Chanel Expands Support for M+ in Extended Partnership

SARAH SZE ,

Centrifuge , 2017, mirrors, wood, bamboo, stainless steel, archival pigment prints, ceramic, acrylic paint, salt, suitcase, lights, fans, video projectors, and speaker system, dimensions variable. Courtesy and copyright the artist and Victoria Miro, London/Venice.

Hong Kong’s M+ announced on October 21 that French luxury house Chanel has signed on as a lead partner for the visual culture museum, backing its new multiyear project series “Pioneering Visions.” The agreement renews and extends M+’s current partnership with the brand, which began in 2023, for a further three years.

“Pioneering Visions” will incorporate an expansive calendar of exhibitions, public programs, and collection-focused activations highlighting figures such as Kimsooja, Duan Jianyu, Cao Fei, and Yu Ji. As part of the initiative, a solo exhibition of Sarah Sze, titled “Centrifuge,” will open in the museum’s Focus Gallery in February 2027. In keeping with its title, the series intends to highlight fresh perspectives and transformative practices by artists and creatives across Asia and abroad.

Through the Chanel Culture Fund, the brand has supported M+ since the museum’s opening. In 2022, it underwrote the presentation of Mark Cousins’s 14-hour documentary project Women Make Film , along with an accompanying screening and educational seminar series at M+ Cinema. The house became a major partner in 2023, funding the curatorial post of Chanel senior curator, head of moving image, and supporting initiatives including M+ Restored and the Asian Avant-Garde Film Collection to preserve and distribute regional experimental cinema.

Museum director Suhanya Raffel welcomed Chanel’s extended commitment. In a press release, she stated that the collaboration “will provide deeper access to lesser-known stories of significant artists of our time, creating new opportunities for engagement, exchange, and discovery for audiences in Hong Kong and internationally.”

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.
excerpt_original: The French luxury house broadened its commitment from moving image to museum-wide programs. Harison Butler

editorial_excerpt_zh: 《清晨开始的地方》 我相信我们所有人都同时生活在多种时间里：钟表时间、日历时间，以及我们所居住的居家空间的节奏……本文《Jenya Kapitsky》最先发表于《摄影之眼》杂志。

article_text:
Where the Day Begins

I believe we all inhabit several temporalities at once: clock time, calendar time, and the rhythm of the domestic space we live in; perhaps also the tempo of places and people woven into our lives; and, finally, our own interior time—each moving at its own pace. It is this interior time that anchors someone to a particular era, whether past or future. I take photographs as I live, and the images form my view of life itself. I am not trying to invent characters or build a conceptual project. The writer and art theorist Viktor Shklovsky wrote that the purpose of art is to “clean the windows”— to restore our ability to perceive the world, to look upon our surroundings with fresh and defamiliarized eyes. Over time, I have taught myself to recognize whatever in the present rhymes with old photographs, with my own inner pace, and with my grandparents’ generation and to photograph it. This draws me toward an imagined world masquerading as “the old days,” with no specific address. It is the kind of time spoken of in Alice in Wonderland: where the day begins; what lingers after a fairy tale has been told or a song sung; what is left of a jar of jam once it has been eaten. It is a time where smiles and memories are kept, a posture, an embrace, a look, and light falling so beautifully it catches your breath. Some of my photographs are taken without ever making an exposure. They exist only in memory—a fleeting moment that dissolved before the shutter could trip, an encounter when I had no camera in hand, or simply a reluctance to break the quiet grace of a scene by moving. Perhaps this imagined time and non-place are a memory of a happy childhood, a longing for a place where no one can return. But either way, what matters to me is creating a space where people can, metaphorically, rest their head on a shoulder, smile, and feel for a moment that this is not only about me and the world around me, but also, a little, about them, and their own happy moments.

article_text:
Art Review

David Reed Went Where Lichtenstein Wouldn’t

He brought his optical preoccupations into the 21st century, without losing his love of artists from earlier eras.

David Reed: Terrible Idea at Rodder is one of the few instances where the artist has shown his paintings and drawings together, in this case, those dated between 2013 and this year. Reed cites artists as disparate as Barnett Newman, Piero della Francesca, and Giovanni Battista Tiepolo as inspirations for his explorations of the interaction of color in opaque forms, layered transparencies, figure-ground interactions, and more. Along with those artists, he also mentions being influenced by everything from something someone said in his studio to an email regarding a painting he was working on.

In 2010, I spoke to Reed for an interview . In it, he made two statements that came to mind when I saw this exhibition:

My paintings are about process but hide the process. [Milton] Resnick spoke about what he called “studio paintings”.... There are certain paintings that you make for yourself to advance your painting, to find out about painting, to do something different and new. I decided that I only wanted to make “studio paintings”. I love to get a painting back and re-work it. Also it means they’re strangely open in some sense. I almost feel like I never finish anything.

I want to be a bedroom painter. I like to look at my paintings as I’m falling asleep or waking up. I like the idea that other people would see them that way and would connect them to dreams, half-thoughts and musings, not just analytical thought and put them in that space between dreaming and waking. I think that’s when paintings really enter you and become a part of you.
excerpt_original: He brought his optical preoccupations into the 21st century, without losing his love of artists from earlier eras.

article_text:
À l’occasion de la prochaine édition de Paris Photo , la Fisheye Gallery est fière de présenter une centaine d’épreuves d’époque de l’Agence France-Presse. Si le fonds de l’AFP conserve aujourd’hui plus de six millions de négatifs minutieusement répertoriés, son corpus de tirages originaux d’époque « de presse » s’avère infiniment plus rare et fragmentaire. Cet article, écrit par la galeriste Tess Druot, est à retrouver dans Fisheye #79 .

Envoyées à la hâte aux rédactions du monde entier, ces épreuves étaient rarement restituées : manipulées, découpées, annotées puis souvent perdues ou jetées une fois le journal imprimé, peu d’entre elles ont survécu. À l’ère de la dématérialisation et du flux numérique ininterrompu, ce « patrimoine adventice » [concept forgé par Sandrine Bula, dans In situ – Revue des patrimoines , qui désigne des fonds photographiques entrés de façon fortuite dans les institutions publiques et qui sont devenus des objets d’archive d’une valeur patrimoniale et historique exceptionnelle, ndlr] acquiert une aura nouvelle. Comme le souligne l’historienne de la photographie Clara Bouveresse dans cette même revue, la numérisation des flux ne rend pas le tirage vintage obsolète, elle en révèle au contraire l’extrême rareté et la valeur de collection.

Devoir de mémoire

Préserver ce trésor physique est une chance et un devoir. Ces tirages de presse constituent l’archéologie vivante du geste journalistique. Chaque épreuve raconte deux histoires simultanées : au recto, la saisie précise de l’événement, la maîtrise de la lumière et la pertinence du cadre ; au verso, la vie intime et secrète de l’image. Là où le travail de rédaction laissait ses empreintes (retouches à la gouache, recadrages, papillons de légende), l’épreuve gélatino-argentique dépasse le statut de simple image pour devenir un véritable artefact matériel. Chaque tirage porte en lui les traces physiques, presque charnelles, de l’histoire en train de se faire et de se diffuser. Ce qui nous inspire profondément dans l’exploration de ce fonds d’exception, c’est l’incroyable pluralité des regards qui le compose. Loin d’un simple enregistrement neutre, les photographes de l’agence ont su développer une véritable écriture de l’événement. Au-delà du strict compte-rendu factuel ou de l’urgence de l’information, ils ont su, décennie après décennie, s’approcher au plus près du sujet humain. Beaucoup ont réussi à sortir du cadre purement documentaire pour adopter une écriture graphique, poétique, parfois franchement artistique, sans jamais sacrifier la rigueur ni la vérité de l’information. Cette sélection illustre la bascule fascinante où l’outil de presse d’hier accède pleinement au rang d’œuvre d’art, rendant ainsi hommage à la vitalité d’une institution séculaire, qui continue de façonner notre imaginaire visuel. Afin de rendre grâce à la double nature d’objet d’art et d’archive de ces pièces d’exception, chaque tirage présenté sur notre stand sera sublimé par un encadrement sur-mesure : un montage entre-deux-verres pensé comme un dispositif d’immersion, permettant d’en apprécier toute la matérialité, du recto jusqu’au verso.

Dans le cadre du Bicentenaire, la RATP et Fisheye s’associent à l’AFP pour dévoiler une trentaine de tirages originaux dans de nombreuses gares et stations du réseau jusqu’au 20 janvier 2027. Pour parfaire cette mise en lumière, Fisheye Éditions publie un ouvrage inédit qui sera lancé dans un premier temps à Paris Photo puis disponible sur Fisheye Store courant novembre.

Retrouvez la Fisheye Gallery à Paris Photo, dans le secteur « Principal », stand D45, du 12 au 15 novembre 2026.

が9月18日〜11月8日に開催されている。", "links": [{"text": "京都・亀岡保津川公園", "url": "https://www.tokyoartbeat.com/venues/-/Kyoto-Kameoka-Hozugawa-Park"}, {"text": "「ART PARK PROGRAM」", "url": "ここでは、美術評論家の三木学が「万博後」の芸術祭や建築を見据える視点から本イベントをレビュー。前編では、イベントの成り立ちと農小屋プロジェクト「Bricoyage」の10作品を論じる。【Tokyo Art Beat】"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "＊後編は こちら", "links": [{"text": "こちら", "url": "https://www.tokyoartbeat.com/articles/-/art-park-program-review-2-202610"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "【後編】民藝から里藝へ──万博後の亀岡から考えるアートと建築。京都「ART PARK PROGRAM」レビュー（評：三木学）"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "京都・亀岡保津川公園で野外アートイベント「ART PARK PROGRAM」が11月8日まで開催中。美術評論家の三木学が「万博後」の視点から本イベントを読み解くレビューを前後編でお届け（撮影：井上嘉和）"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/4b265737/c6104a42-b9d2-478c-a687-546877f477b5.jpg?w=639&q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "＊本展のレポート記事は こちら", "links": [{"text": "こちら", "url": "https://www.tokyoartbeat.com/articles/-/art-park-program-report-202610"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "秋の京都・亀岡で、人と自然が交差する芸術体験を。「ART PARK PROGRAM」の野外アート展示＆農小屋プロジェクトをレポート"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "京都・亀岡保津川公園で野外アートイベント「ART PARK PROGRAM」が開幕。アーティストや建築家らが土地の記憶や自然環境と向き合い制作した作品が、14ヘクタールの広大な土地に広がる（撮影：佐々木明日華）"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/54eedbad/3337df23-ff04-428e-8d24-be81d52dda90.jpg?w=639&q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "アートと食の地産地消"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大阪・関西万博の翌年であり、2027年に横浜で開かれる「国際園芸博覧会（GREEN×EXPO 2027）」の前年にあたる今年、京都府亀岡市などを舞台に「第43回全国都市緑化フェアin京都丹波」が開かれている。そのメイン会場のひとつ、京都・亀岡保津川公園で展開されているのが「ART PARK PROGRAM」である。万博とは比較にならない小さな試みだが、そこには万博後の芸術祭や建築が向かうひとつの方向が示されている。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "JR亀岡駅は京都駅から快速で20分ほど、保津川下りの起点の町である。北口を出て5分も歩けば、畦の残る田園が広がる。約14ヘクタールの会場には、野外アート展示「Art Sprout（アート・スプラウト）」、農小屋プロジェクト「Bricoyage（ブリコヤージュ）」、市民育成プログラム「ハラッパー」の3つからなるART PARK PROGRAMのほか、建築家・大野宏による竹と稲藁の作品群、台湾の工芸チームによる竹の作品などが点在している。会場を設計した高野ランドスケーププランニングと一般社団法人ランドスケープコンサルタンツ協会は、そのテーマを「里藝（さとげい）」と名づけた。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/b906a0d8/0fd4302d-840e-4517-99cc-860ed7e68847.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "京都・亀岡保津川公園内にある崔石鎬《再会》", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "亀岡には以前から、京都の美術大学を卒業した多くのアーティストがアトリエを構えてきた。しかし発表の場は主に市外にあり、 桂川孝裕市長 は 「芸術家はここで作品を作って、全部都会や海外で発表してたんです」 と振り返る。アートは地元で生産されながら地元では消費されない「輸出品」だったのである。それを地域につなぐために2018年に始まったのが「かめおか霧の芸術祭」であり、亀岡在住の陶芸家で総合プロデューサーを務める松井利夫らが切り開いてきたその活動を、今回のフェアは集約するものだという。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "亀岡は霧の町として知られる。晩秋から初春の晴れた夜、放射冷却で冷えた空気が周囲の山々から流れ下って盆地の底に溜まり、風が遮られるため日が高くなるまで盆地を覆い続ける。いわゆる丹波霧である。視界を奪い交通を妨げる霧をあえて芸術祭の名に掲げたのは、それを負の条件ではなく土地の個性としてとらえ直すためであった。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "駅南口には、30年ほど前から亀岡に制作拠点を構えるヤノベケンジの《SHIP'S CAT MISTY》が設置され、駅の北側から会場にかけては、西野康造、崔石鎬、山口牧生ら亀岡ゆかりの作家の彫刻が来訪者を導いている。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/9e870bd2/9db55bde-ab0a-4a9e-a428-1b123e91d704.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "亀岡駅南口にあるヤノベケンジ《SHIP'S CAT MISTY》", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "地域外から作家を招いて滞在制作させる芸術祭が定型となったなかで、亀岡の出発点は、すでにこの土地で制作している人々の存在にある。それは企画する側にも及ぶ。Bricoyageを企画する 農小屋学会 に加わり、ハラッパーのディレクターを務める 辰巳雄基 は亀岡に拠点を構え、Art Sproutのディレクターである 野田智子（Nadegata Instant Party） は、亀岡にルーツをもつパートナーの 山城大督 とともにTwelve Inc.を経営している。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/760503dc/6a5cb8d0-ad06-49e7-a68f-6fd539ab326c.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "「ART PARK PROGRAM」の市民育成プログラム「ハラッパー」の参加者", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "会場そのものにも来歴がある。一帯はもともと京都サンガF.C.のスタジアム建設予定地だったが、国の天然記念物である淡水魚アユモドキの産卵場所があったことから、2016年に建設位置が駅のすぐ北側へ変更された。現在のサンガスタジアム by KYOCERAである。残された広大な市有地では、アユモドキの保全と有機農業が結びつき、有機農家や研究者による田植えが始まった。市は2023年に「オーガニックビレッジ」を宣言し、有機農法の市民学校の運営を株式会社ビオかめおかに委託している。作られた有機米は、地元の子供たちの給食に使用されており、出口まで設計されているのだ。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "田んぼで生まれるプランクトンがアユモドキの餌になるという連鎖を語りながら、市長は 「これも循環ですよ」 と語った。市はさらにこの土地を京都・亀岡保津川公園として整備し、緑化フェアを誘致した。市長によれば、大阪・関西万博と横浜の園芸博覧会の「間の谷間」にあたる年の開催地が決まっていないことを知り、国に働きかけたという。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "芸術祭のために場所が作られたのではなく、土地の使い方を考え続けてきた循環のなかに、アートがつながった。亀岡で生まれたアートが亀岡の人々に届く。食と芸術のふたつの「地産地消」が、同じ駅北の田園で重なり合っているのだ。"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "造園家の視線と「里藝」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "桂川市長は東京農業大学で造園を学び、高校で造園を教えたのち市職員に転じ、自らを「造園家の政治家」であると語る。「田園はそれ自体美しいが、作品というフォーカルポイントを置くことで空間が締まり、背後の風景が生きてくる。ここは借景を生かした庭なんですよね」と述べた。会場設計も既存の田畑の区画割を尊重し、畦をそのまま動線にしている。来場者は農道を歩くように会場を巡り、その途中で作品に出会う。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "「里藝」は、柳宗悦らが1920年代に提唱した「民藝」を踏まえた言葉で、設計者たちはそれを、特別な誰かひとりが作る作品ではなく、多くの命と時間が織りなしてきた土地の創造だと説明する。民藝も「良い工芸は土地の材料と風土から生まれる」と考えたが、その眼差しは最終的に、蒐集され陳列される「もの」に向かった。里藝は、竹細工を支える竹林と手入れする人、藁を生む稲作と編む手まで含めて、「もの」が土地から生まれ、やがて土地へ還る循環そのものを対象にしている。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "もっとも、会場に並ぶのは名のある作家の作品である。しかし民藝運動もまた、無名の工人を称揚しながら濱田庄司や河井寬次郎を生んだ。その逆説を引き受けるように、ここでの作品の多くは、畦や水路、竹林や稲藁といった無名の土地の創造を見えるようにする装置として働いている。作品はいわば、里藝という無名の営みへの入口なのである。"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "建築家なしの建築、農小屋から学ぶ「Bricoyage」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "「ART PARK PROGRAM」において、もっとも土地に根ざした方法をとっているのが、農小屋プロジェクト「Bricoyage」である。ブリコラージュ（寄せ集めて作る、自分で修繕する）とボヤージュ（旅）を合わせた造語で、「小屋」の響きも重なる。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "公募で選ばれた建築家や招聘作家、企画・制作を担う農小屋学会による計10棟の農小屋が点在している。農小屋学会は、辰巳雄基ら4人によるリサーチ組織で、亀岡の300以上の農機具小屋を巡り、2020年に『小屋の本―霧のまち亀岡からみる風景―』（出版：一般社団法人きりぶえ、協力：かめおか霧の芸術祭実行委員会）を出版している。見た目だけでなく、使われ方や建てるプロセスにこそ小屋の魅力があると考えてきた人々が、この企画の土台にいる。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "農小屋は、建築家が設計したものではない。農具を置き、休み、雨風をしのぐ必要に応じて、農家が手近な木材や波板、古材で作り、壊れれば直し、足りなければ足す。関東大震災後のバラックを記録した今和次郎の考現学や、バーナード・ルドフスキーの言う「建築家なしの建築」とも並べて考えられるだろう。しかも会場は湿地を含む農地であり、法規上、基礎と屋根を備えた通常の建築物を自由に建てることはできない。万博の仮設建築よりさらに弱い、「建築擬き（もどき）」とでも呼ぶべき条件である。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "農小屋学会の《インフォメーション小屋》は、廃木材の柱やトタン、刈られた草など、そこにある素材で作られた案内所兼休憩所兼資材置き場である。2400mmのグリッドで立てた柱に、必要な機能を後から足していける。暑ければタープを掛け、座る場所が要れば柱をつないでベンチにする。資材置き場には亀岡の材料がストックされ、来場者も痕跡を残していく。来るたびに風景が変わるという農小屋の性格が、ここでは設計の原理になっている。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/0fdd5534/1660d919-016c-4071-8c6a-cd880fd8f3c6.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "会場風景より、農小屋学会《インフォメーション小屋》", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "studio-L＋関西学院大学山崎亮研究室の《公小屋》は、図書館で廃棄される本棚を再利用して、公園の「公」を問い直している。中国から伝わった「公」は市民がそれぞれ少しずつ「私」を開き、みんなで作りあげることを意味していたが、日本では地域を管理する豪族を指す「おおやけ」に置き換わったという。公園を「おおやけ」的に考えれば役所が禁止事項を決めて管理する場所になり、「公」的に考えれば市民が集まり活動する場所になる。フェア後の公園はどちらを目指すのか、と作品は問いかける。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/0e61b8dd/2a2c3f57-36b8-4777-99e6-f53373c25287.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "会場風景より、studio-L＋関西学院大学山崎亮研究室《公小屋》", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "敷地の土とモルタル、草が混ぜられた素材の小屋の本棚には、五穀、滝、山、猪、鹿、かかしといった名を墨で記した割り木の札が並び、春分と秋分の西日の線上に開けられた窓からは、家々と稲穂、電車が見える。あらゆるものに神が見出されてきた日本で、それはスマートフォンのような現在の「もの」にもいえるのではないかと山崎亮は語る。まだ名のない札も多く、会期中に過去と現在の神様が集められ、アーカイヴが育っていくという。管理されるのを待つのではなく、無数の「もの」に宿る神を名指し、場に関わり続けること。それが「公」の公園への第一歩なのかもしれない。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "山崎はランドスケープアーキテクトとして出発し、人や共同体をデザインするコミュニティデザインを提唱するようになった。2013年の瀬戸内国際芸術祭では、小豆島の醤の郷で醤油の容器を用いたインスタレーションを地域住民とともに発表している。人や共同体をデザインするにも「もの」が要る。山崎のコミュニティデザインもまた、人と「もの」の新たな循環を描いている。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展示設計や仮設建築を手がけ、簡易な施工まで自ら行うドットアーキテクツは、2016年のヴェネチア・ビエンナーレ国際建築展日本館への出展などで知られ、2013年の瀬戸内国際芸術祭でも集会所を設計・施工している。今回は、ハラッパーたちが実際に使う農小屋を参照し、パブリックな農小屋として《亀岡の小屋》を制作した。木の柱と梁による簡素な休憩所の上には、「FARMING ON COMMON LAND」という大きな看板文字が掲げられている。共有地で耕すという言葉は《公小屋》の問いとも響き合い、目の前の田んぼを保津川の流域全体へ、みんなの土地へと開いていく。ここで建築家はかたちを上から与える存在ではなく、農家が作ってきたものから建築を学び直しているのである。"}, {"type": "image", "url": article_text:
京都・丹波地域の複数エリアで行われている「第43回全国都市緑化フェアin京都丹波」。そのメイン会場のひとつである 京都・亀岡保津川公園 で、野外アートイベント 「ART PARK PROGRAM」 が9月18日〜11月8日に開催されている。

広大な公園・農地という開かれた場所で多様な作品が点在する本イベントでは、アート、農小屋、市民チーム活動という3つのアプローチから、土地や自然の歴史、人の営みと向き合い、それぞれが共鳴しながらこの場所ならでは風景を作り上げている。

ここでは、美術評論家の三木学が「万博後」の芸術祭や建築を見据える視点から本イベントをレビュー。前編では、イベントの成り立ちと農小屋プロジェクト「Bricoyage」の10作品を論じる。【Tokyo Art Beat】

＊後編は こちら

【後編】民藝から里藝へ──万博後の亀岡から考えるアートと建築。京都「ART PARK PROGRAM」レビュー（評：三木学）

京都・亀岡保津川公園で野外アートイベント「ART PARK PROGRAM」が11月8日まで開催中。美術評論家の三木学が「万博後」の視点から本イベントを読み解くレビューを前後編でお届け（撮影：井上嘉和）

＊本展のレポート記事は こちら

秋の京都・亀岡で、人と自然が交差する芸術体験を。「ART PARK PROGRAM」の野外アート展示＆農小屋プロジェクトをレポート

京都・亀岡保津川公園で野外アートイベント「ART PARK PROGRAM」が開幕。アーティストや建築家らが土地の記憶や自然環境と向き合い制作した作品が、14ヘクタールの広大な土地に広がる（撮影：佐々木明日華）

アートと食の地産地消

大阪・関西万博の翌年であり、2027年に横浜で開かれる「国際園芸博覧会（GREEN×EXPO 2027）」の前年にあたる今年、京都府亀岡市などを舞台に「第43回全国都市緑化フェアin京都丹波」が開かれている。そのメイン会場のひとつ、京都・亀岡保津川公園で展開されているのが「ART PARK PROGRAM」である。万博とは比較にならない小さな試みだが、そこには万博後の芸術祭や建築が向かうひとつの方向が示されている。

JR亀岡駅は京都駅から快速で20分ほど、保津川下りの起点の町である。北口を出て5分も歩けば、畦の残る田園が広がる。約14ヘクタールの会場には、野外アート展示「Art Sprout（アート・スプラウト）」、農小屋プロジェクト「Bricoyage（ブリコヤージュ）」、市民育成プログラム「ハラッパー」の3つからなるART PARK PROGRAMのほか、建築家・大野宏による竹と稲藁の作品群、台湾の工芸チームによる竹の作品などが点在している。会場を設計した高野ランドスケーププランニングと一般社団法人ランドスケープコンサルタンツ協会は、そのテーマを「里藝（さとげい）」と名づけた。

亀岡には以前から、京都の美術大学を卒業した多くのアーティストがアトリエを構えてきた。しかし発表の場は主に市外にあり、 桂川孝裕市長 は 「芸術家はここで作品を作って、全部都会や海外で発表してたんです」 と振り返る。アートは地元で生産されながら地元では消費されない「輸出品」だったのである。それを地域につなぐために2018年に始まったのが「かめおか霧の芸術祭」であり、亀岡在住の陶芸家で総合プロデューサーを務める松井利夫らが切り開いてきたその活動を、今回のフェアは集約するものだという。

亀岡は霧の町として知られる。晩秋から初春の晴れた夜、放射冷却で冷えた空気が周囲の山々から流れ下って盆地の底に溜まり、風が遮られるため日が高くなるまで盆地を覆い続ける。いわゆる丹波霧である。視界を奪い交通を妨げる霧をあえて芸術祭の名に掲げたのは、それを負の条件ではなく土地の個性としてとらえ直すためであった。

駅南口には、30年ほど前から亀岡に制作拠点を構えるヤノベケンジの《SHIP'S CAT MISTY》が設置され、駅の北側から会場にかけては、西野康造、崔石鎬、山口牧生ら亀岡ゆかりの作家の彫刻が来訪者を導いている。

地域外から作家を招いて滞在制作させる芸術祭が定型となったなかで、亀岡の出発点は、すでにこの土地で制作している人々の存在にある。それは企画する側にも及ぶ。Bricoyageを企画する 農小屋学会 に加わり、ハラッパーのディレクターを務める 辰巳雄基 は亀岡に拠点を構え、Art Sproutのディレクターである 野田智子（Nadegata Instant Party） は、亀岡にルーツをもつパートナーの 山城大督 とともにTwelve Inc.を経営している。

会場そのものにも来歴がある。一帯はもともと京都サンガF.C.のスタジアム建設予定地だったが、国の天然記念物である淡水魚アユモドキの産卵場所があったことから、2016年に建設位置が駅のすぐ北側へ変更された。現在のサンガスタジアム by KYOCERAである。残された広大な市有地では、アユモドキの保全と有機農業が結びつき、有機農家や研究者による田植えが始まった。市は2023年に「オーガニックビレッジ」を宣言し、有機農法の市民学校の運営を株式会社ビオかめおかに委託している。作られた有機米は、地元の子供たちの給食に使用されており、出口まで設計されているのだ。

田んぼで生まれるプランクトンがアユモドキの餌になるという連鎖を語りながら、市長は 「これも循環ですよ」 と語った。市はさらにこの土地を京都・亀岡保津川公園として整備し、緑化フェアを誘致した。市長によれば、大阪・関西万博と横浜の園芸博覧会の「間の谷間」にあたる年の開催地が決まっていないことを知り、国に働きかけたという。

芸術祭のために場所が作られたのではなく、土地の使い方を考え続けてきた循環のなかに、アートがつながった。亀岡で生まれたアートが亀岡の人々に届く。食と芸術のふたつの「地産地消」が、同じ駅北の田園で重なり合っているのだ。

造園家の視線と「里藝」

桂川市長は東京農業大学で造園を学び、高校で造園を教えたのち市職員に転じ、自らを「造園家の政治家」であると語る。「田園はそれ自体美しいが、作品というフォーカルポイントを置くことで空間が締まり、背後の風景が生きてくる。ここは借景を生かした庭なんですよね」と述べた。会場設計も既存の田畑の区画割を尊重し、畦をそのまま動線にしている。来場者は農道を歩くように会場を巡り、その途中で作品に出会う。

「里藝」は、柳宗悦らが1920年代に提唱した「民藝」を踏まえた言葉で、設計者たちはそれを、特別な誰かひとりが作る作品ではなく、多くの命と時間が織りなしてきた土地の創造だと説明する。民藝も「良い工芸は土地の材料と風土から生まれる」と考えたが、その眼差しは最終的に、蒐集され陳列される「もの」に向かった。里藝は、竹細工を支える竹林と手入れする人、藁を生む稲作と編む手まで含めて、「もの」が土地から生まれ、やがて土地へ還る循環そのものを対象にしている。

もっとも、会場に並ぶのは名のある作家の作品である。しかし民藝運動もまた、無名の工人を称揚しながら濱田庄司や河井寬次郎を生んだ。その逆説を引き受けるように、ここでの作品の多くは、畦や水路、竹林や稲藁といった無名の土地の創造を見えるようにする装置として働いている。作品はいわば、里藝という無名の営みへの入口なのである。

建築家なしの建築、農小屋から学ぶ「Bricoyage」

「ART PARK PROGRAM」において、もっとも土地に根ざした方法をとっているのが、農小屋プロジェクト「Bricoyage」である。ブリコラージュ（寄せ集めて作る、自分で修繕する）とボヤージュ（旅）を合わせた造語で、「小屋」の響きも重なる。

公募で選ばれた建築家や招聘作家、企画・制作を担う農小屋学会による計10棟の農小屋が点在している。農小屋学会は、辰巳雄基ら4人によるリサーチ組織で、亀岡の300以上の農機具小屋を巡り、2020年に『小屋の本―霧のまち亀岡からみる風景―』（出版：一般社団法人きりぶえ、協力：かめおか霧の芸術祭実行委員会）を出版している。見た目だけでなく、使われ方や建てるプロセスにこそ小屋の魅力があると考えてきた人々が、この企画の土台にいる。

農小屋は、建築家が設計したものではない。農具を置き、休み、雨風をしのぐ必要に応じて、農家が手近な木材や波板、古材で作り、壊れれば直し、足りなければ足す。関東大震災後のバラックを記録した今和次郎の考現学や、バーナード・ルドフスキーの言う「建築家なしの建築」とも並べて考えられるだろう。しかも会場は湿地を含む農地であり、法規上、基礎と屋根を備えた通常の建築物を自由に建てることはできない。万博の仮設建築よりさらに弱い、「建築擬き（もどき）」とでも呼ぶべき条件である。

農小屋学会の《インフォメーション小屋》は、廃木材の柱やトタン、刈られた草など、そこにある素材で作られた案内所兼休憩所兼資材置き場である。2400mmのグリッドで立てた柱に、必要な機能を後から足していける。暑ければタープを掛け、座る場所が要れば柱をつないでベンチにする。資材置き場には亀岡の材料がストックされ、来場者も痕跡を残していく。来るたびに風景が変わるという農小屋の性格が、ここでは設計の原理になっている。

studio-L＋関西学院大学山崎亮研究室の《公小屋》は、図書館で廃棄される本棚を再利用して、公園の「公」を問い直している。中国から伝わった「公」は市民がそれぞれ少しずつ「私」を開き、みんなで作りあげることを意味していたが、日本では地域を管理する豪族を指す「おおやけ」に置き換わったという。公園を「おおやけ」的に考えれば役所が禁止事項を決めて管理する場所になり、「公」的に考えれば市民が集まり活動する場所になる。フェア後の公園はどちらを目指すのか、と作品は問いかける。

敷地の土とモルタル、草が混ぜられた素材の小屋の本棚には、五穀、滝、山、猪、鹿、かかしといった名を墨で記した割り木の札が並び、春分と秋分の西日の線上に開けられた窓からは、家々と稲穂、電車が見える。あらゆるものに神が見出されてきた日本で、それはスマートフォンのような現在の「もの」にもいえるのではないかと山崎亮は語る。まだ名のない札も多く、会期中に過去と現在の神様が集められ、アーカイヴが育っていくという。管理されるのを待つのではなく、無数の「もの」に宿る神を名指し、場に関わり続けること。それが「公」の公園への第一歩なのかもしれない。

山崎はランドスケープアーキテクトとして出発し、人や共同体をデザインするコミュニティデザインを提唱するようになった。2013年の瀬戸内国際芸術祭では、小豆島の醤の郷で醤油の容器を用いたインスタレーションを地域住民とともに発表している。人や共同体をデザインするにも「もの」が要る。山崎のコミュニティデザインもまた、人と「もの」の新たな循環を描いている。

展示設計や仮設建築を手がけ、簡易な施工まで自ら行うドットアーキテクツは、2016年のヴェネチア・ビエンナーレ国際建築展日本館への出展などで知られ、2013年の瀬戸内国際芸術祭でも集会所を設計・施工している。今回は、ハラッパーたちが実際に使う農小屋を参照し、パブリックな農小屋として《亀岡の小屋》を制作した。木の柱と梁による簡素な休憩所の上には、「FARMING ON COMMON LAND」という大きな看板文字が掲げられている。共有地で耕すという言葉は《公小屋》の問いとも響き合い、目の前の田んぼを保津川の流域全体へ、みんなの土地へと開いていく。ここで建築家はかたちを上から与える存在ではなく、農家が作ってきたものから建築を学び直しているのである。

周囲の環境を見つめ、視点を転回させる実践

風×土 設計共同体の《用美の畝》は、機械を使わず多くの人の手で掘った井戸の小屋で、地下水や地層という普段見えないものを露わにする。間（あわい）の竹のドーム《発芽》は、京都伝統工芸大学校で竹を学ぶ若い作り手と長く竹の仕事に携わってきた職人による、世代横断型のユニットの作品である。亀岡の放置竹林を整備しながら切り出した竹を割り、「やたら編み」で、種から芽が空へ伸びるような曲面を作った。すべてを手作業で行うことで、竹資源の循環や竹林の管理につなげたいという。

ピメシャラ《様子見の小屋》は、その名のとおり完成を急がない。飛騨高山などを拠点とする設計チームは、自然の振る舞いを観察する「様子見」の時間こそが必要だと考え、月に一度亀岡に滞在しながら「場当たり的」に小屋を建てていく。隣の畑を営む人々との竹採りから始まり、麦農家から譲り受けた麦藁が屋根となり、地元の製材所の丸太や廃材の農業用パイプが加わる。版築や麦藁葺きには興味をもった人々の手が加わり、小屋は会期中も旅を続けている。「Bricoyage」という名にもっとも素直に応えている小屋かもしれない。

いっぽう、ローランド・ハーゲンバーグ《HOUSE OF HEART》は、素材の来歴をそのまま見せるほかの小屋とは対照的である。1980年代のニューヨークでウォーホルやバスキアを撮った写真家として知られ、京都に暮らすハーゲンバーグは、木材を白く塗って素材の表情を消し、「家」の輪郭だけを田園に置いて、その内側にハートを象った白い梁を組んだ。人は中に入れない。住むための家ではなく、見るための家である。無数の白いフレームは、季節や時刻によって影を変えながら、周囲の田園をさまざまなカットに切り取る。どのフレームで風景を見るかは、来場者が自ら選ぶことになる。写真家は現実を心打たれるフレームに切り取る。ハーゲンバーグは写真家という出自を活かし、カメラのない写真の家を築いたといえるかもしれない。

「Bricoyage」でも出色なのは、村上慧《多すぎず、少なすぎないように》だろう。駅の北側には田園風景が広がるが、南側には新興の住宅地がある。会場から駅の方向を見ると、エネルギー効率と経済効率を極限まで追求した箱型の街並みが目に入る。村上は、その無機質な壁面を横倒しにしたような小屋を作り、中央のプランターに枇杷の木を植えた。農小屋ではなく、近年普及している箱型の家に注目したのも、村上自身がアーティストとして発泡スチロールで最小限の家を作り、日本中を旅していたことと無関係ではないだろう。村上は、そこで日記を書き本にしているが、まさに鴨長明の「方丈庵」の現代版であり、そこで書かれた随筆『方丈記』といえる。村上の作品も一種の借景である。自然のなかにある住宅と、住宅のなかにある自然という入れ子が、そこにできあがっている。

民具を救出し収集する民具BANKの参加も見逃せない。彼らは失われていく道具を、長年蓄積された身体技法を格納する記憶装置としてとらえている。民具を失うことは、映像記録のなかった時代の身体史や感覚史、身体知を失うことにほかならない。民藝が美の基準で選び取った器や家具とは異なり、民具は美醜を問わず、使い手自身が作った道具まで含む。農小屋もまた、その延長線上にある。

民具BANKの《化かし化かされる緑の庭》は、人間中心の視点から「雑草」と呼ばれてきた植物たちを見直し、周辺の土壌まで含めた環境を組み直している。河野美紀＋榊原真歩《水路の洗濯小屋》も、水路に溜まった泥やゴミをすくいあげる「どぶさらい」をモチーフに、それを屋根にしている。名指しされてこなかったもの、捨てられてきたものの価値を発見し、転回させる操作が、会場の至るところで行われているのだ。

title_original: French Collector François Pinault Plans Permanent Hang in Venice Museum
editorial_title_zh: 法国收藏家弗朗索瓦·皮诺计划在威尼斯博物馆举办常设展
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这位90岁的收藏家计划于2027年3月在威尼斯格拉西宫举办他的首场常设展，展出54位艺术家的106件艺术品。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "90岁的收藏家、开云集团（Kering）奢侈品综合企业及Artémis投资控股公司创始人弗朗索瓦·皮诺（François Pinault）并未变年轻。因此，人们很难不联想这是否促成了他在接受《世界报》（Le Monde）罕见采访时发布的新公告：他计划在其两家威尼斯博物馆之一、装饰华丽的格拉西宫（Palazzo Grassi）举办一场首期常设展，展出其收藏的超过10,000件艺术品中的一部分，开展时间为2027年3月。", "links": [{"text": "Le Monde", "url": "https://www.lemonde.fr/culture/article/2026/10/15/francois-pinault-homme-d-affaires-ma-collection-d-art-est-constituee-a-l-instinct-a-la-passion-ou-meme-a-la-colere-face-aux-violences-du-present_6794076_3246.html?lmd_medium=al&lmd_campaign=envoye-par-appli&lmd_creation=ios&lmd_source=mail"}, {"text": "Palazzo Grassi", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/palazzo-grassi/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该展览将呈现54位艺术家的106件重要艺术品。通常情况下，建于2006年的格拉西宫举办的都是临时展览，这与皮诺的其他两处场馆——巴黎的皮诺收藏-商业交易所（Bourse de Commerce）和威尼斯的海关大楼美术馆（Punta della Dogana）一样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "皮诺没有明确讨论他的传承问题，但在其藏品的管理权方面，目前尚不清楚谁将步其后尘。他确实表示，举办常设展的想法已经酝酿了一段时间，这与人们对传统临时展览无法充分展现其藏品全貌的担忧有关。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他解释道：“到目前为止，公众只能随着展览的来去，零星地发现这段历史。常设展能够将不同时期和不同代际的作品并置，并展示出在独特性之外，某些问题是如何绵延不续的。”基于这一点，他希望永久展出那些“凭借自身力量和经受时间考验的能力而确立了地位”的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不过，皮诺提醒人们，不要以为他就此停止了收藏，也不要认为这个常设展就是他的最终定论。“这绝不是要将收藏凝固，也不是要对其做出最终的解读。我们对艺术的看法在不断演变，”他指的是自己和他的策展团队。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "借此机会，皮诺还透露了他的一些艺术观点。多年来，这些观点让他赢得了涉足具有挑战性的极当代（ultra-contemporary）作品的声誉。“我的收藏极具主观性，往往建立在直觉、激情之上，甚至在面对当下的暴力时会感到愤怒，”他说道，并补充称他对“艺术品能够揭示我们时代的深刻不稳定性”的方式“很敏感”。然而，他将这一点扩展到了那些也“背离[当下]以试图体现无形之物——即超越现实之物”的艺术品，这位提醒人们他经常想起自己作为贫穷农村农民儿子的简陋出身的人补充道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "皮诺是法国罕见的一流收藏家，他倾向于关注在大型博物馆中备受忽视的边缘化和非西方背景艺术家，尽管他坚称自己在看一件艺术品时，绝不关注“护照或性别”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他说：“我的兴趣更多是由与非凡的、几乎具有萨满气质的人物（如大卫·哈蒙斯）的相遇所驱动的。将这个非裔美国人艺术圈带入大众视野，邀请我们走出西方艺术的康庄大道，去走那条少有人走的路。”", "translated": true}]

article_text:
At age 90, collector François Pinault, founder of the Kering luxury conglomerate and the investment holding company Artémis, isn’t getting any younger. So it’s hard not to wonder how that may have factored into his latest announcement in a rare interview with Le Monde , stating he plans to mount a first permanent exhibition from his collection of over 10,000 artworks, opening in March, 2027 at one of his two Venice museums, the ornate Palazzo Grassi .

The display will feature 106 major artworks by 54 artists. Typically, the 2006-founded Palazzo Grassi hosts temporary shows, just like Pinault’s two other venues: the Bourse de Commerce in Paris, and the Punta della Dogana in Venice.

Pinault didn’t explicitly discuss his legacy, but when it comes to the stewardship of his collection, it remains unclear who will follow in his footsteps. He did say that the idea for a permanent hang has been brewing for some time, and has to do with concerns that his traditionally temporary shows don’t give a full-enough picture of his collection.

“Until now, the public has only been able to discover this story in fragments, as exhibitions came and went,” he explained. “A permanent display makes it possible to set works from different periods and generations side by side and to show how, beyond their singularity, certain questions endure.” With that in mind, he hopes to permanently showcase works that “have asserted themselves through their strength and their ability to withstand the passage of time.”

However, Pinault cautioned against assuming he was wrapping up his collecting, or that the permanent show served as his final word. “It is in no way a matter of freezing the collection or offering a definitive reading of it. Our view of art continues to evolve,” he said, referring to himself and his team of curators.

On that note, Pinault also offered a few insights into said view, which, over the years, has earned him a reputation for venturing toward challenging ultra-contemporary works. “My collection is eminently subjective and very often built on instinct, passion, or even anger in the face of the violence of the present,” he said, adding he was “sensitive to the way works of art can reveal the profound instability” of our times. However, he broadened this to include artworks that also “turn away from [the present] in an attempt to embody the invisible — that which precisely transcends reality,” added the man who reminds us that he often thinks of his modest beginnings as the son of a poor rural farmer.

Pinault is a rare top collector in France to gravitate toward artists of marginalized and non-Western backgrounds, who have been under-recognized in major museums, though he insists that when looking at an artwork, he pays no attention to “the passport or gender.”

“My interest has rather been motivated by encounters with extraordinary, almost shamanic figures, like David Hammons,” he said. “Bringing this African-American scene to light invites us to step off the well-trodden paths of Western art and take the road less traveled.”
excerpt_original: The 90-year-old collector is planning a first permanent exhibition of 106 artworks by 54 artists at the Palazzo Grassi in Venice, opening in March 2027.
